answer:
**Short answer:** the reports disagree, because they test different things. Gemma 3 finds almost no quality cost when it measures perplexity. GLM-5 finds a large cost on long-context tasks when the windowed layers are placed naively, and a much smaller one when they are chosen carefully. Mistral 7B uses sliding windows but never measures their effect on quality. Phi-4 drops the sliding window and does not say why. Page numbers below are the PDF pages; for GLM-5 and Gemma 3 they match the printed page numbers.

### Mistral 7B: adopts it, gives no quality ablation
- Each token attends to at most W = 4096 tokens in the previous layer. Because layers stack, tokens outside the window still affect the prediction, giving a theoretical attention span of about 131K tokens (p. 2).
- The stated benefits are cost: about 2x speed over vanilla attention at 16K sequence length (p. 2), and a fixed-size rolling-buffer cache (p. 2).
- The report only claims, in general terms, that the attention mechanisms "contribute to the enhanced performance and efficiency" (p. 1). It contains no experiment isolating the window's effect on quality.

### Gemma 3: little to no cost in perplexity
- Gemma 3 uses 5 local sliding-window layers for every global layer (p. 2), with a 1024-token window in its architecture (p. 7, Fig. 6).
- Changing the local:global ratio has "minimal impact on perplexity", even at 7:1 (p. 6, Fig. 3).
- "The sliding window can be reduced significantly without impacting perplexity," tested from 512 to 4096 tokens (pp. 6–7, Fig. 4).
- The gain is memory: KV-cache overhead falls from 60% with global-only attention to under 15% with a 1:3 ratio and sw=1024, at a 32K context (p. 7, Fig. 5).
- Caveats: these ablations use 2B/9B text-only models and validation perplexity (pp. 6–7). They are not long-context task benchmarks.

### Phi-4: drops it, no reason given
- Phi-4 uses "full attention over the 4K context length, rather than a 2K sliding window used in phi-3-medium" (p. 7). There is no ablation or explanation, so the report doesn't show whether the window hurt quality.

### GLM-5: large long-context cost unless layers are chosen well
- On a GLM-9B base with a 128K context, the authors convert half the layers to SWA (1:1 ratio, 4096-token window) (pp. 6–7).
- **Without retraining** (RULER, Table 4, p. 7):
  - With a fixed alternating pattern, scores collapse at long lengths: 54.02 against 93.67 for full attention at the second length tested, and 6.51 against 75.28 at 128K.
  - With layers picked by beam search, scores stay much closer: 92.54 and 53.95 at those lengths.
- **After continued training** (Table 5, p. 7):
  - With the alternating pattern, RULER@128K drops by 30.35 points, which the authors call "catastrophic degradation" on long-context tasks.
  - With search-based layer selection, the drop on the same benchmark is 5.69 points. Drops on the other benchmarks are 1.81, 2.76 and 14.66 at 128K.
- GLM-5 itself uses DeepSeek Sparse Attention instead, which picks tokens based on content "unlike fixed patterns (like sliding windows)" (p. 5).

### Overall
Measured by short-context perplexity, sliding windows cost almost nothing, even with small windows and high local ratios (Gemma 3, pp. 6–7). Measured by long-context retrieval and reasoning, they can cost a lot, depending heavily on which layers are windowed (GLM-5, p. 7). None of these papers runs both kinds of test on the same model, so the difference may come from the evaluation rather than the method.
